Oil bears seize control in the futures market

Investors have become increasingly bearish about all parts of the petroleum complex (with the exception of U.S. gasoline) as the United States and Iran have signalled a preference to negotiate rather than resume unrestricted warfare.

Hedge funds and other money managers sold the equivalent of 93 million barrels in the six most important futures and options contracts over the seven days ending on November 3.

Fund managers sold petroleum contracts at the fastest rate for more than ten months since before the U.S. military operations against Venezuela and Iran ...

The volume of refined products being loaded within the Persian Gulf is rising, with most of that exiting the Strait of Hormuz and providing some relief to one of the tightest corners of the global oil market nine months into the Iran war.

The region loaded about 3 million barrels a day of distillates including diesel, petrochemical feedstock naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas in October, according to data from ship-tracking and analytics firm Vortexa Ltd. While that’s still only about half of pre-conflict levels, that’s up from a trough in May of about 1 million barrels a day. #oott

#Commodities: 
Oil: Brent has now fallen around 22% from its late-October peak above USD 117, hovering near USD 92 as hopes for an end to the eight-month-old Middle East conflict have strengthened following the US midterm elections. President Trump added to the optimism by suggesting further strikes on Iran would not be necessary. While crude oil flows have almost returned to pre-war levels, LNG and refined product supplies remain constrained, keeping prices elevated, particularly for diesel. A peace deal could help ease these pressures, but for now, European diesel still trades around USD 175 per barrel, while the Dutch TTF gas benchmark has retreated to around EUR 81/MWh from its pre-midterms peak above EUR 104. Focus today: The EIA's Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) and any fresh signals from Washington and Tehran on the prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough.

Metals: Gold trades lower after once again struggling to break resistance near USD 4,170 ahead of today's US CPI release, which carries the risk of reinforcing expectations of a December Fed rate hike. The post-midterm rebound, supported by slumping oil prices and short covering among leveraged funds, has helped stabilise the market. Traders are now weighing whether the next move will be further consolidation above USD 4,000 or renewed gains that could strengthen confidence that a durable low is in place. In my view, the latter would require a sustained break above USD 4,200.

European power prices surge as cold weather and weak renewable output squeeze supplies: An unfortunate combination of colder weather across parts of Europe, the highest natural gas prices since 2022, and a prolonged period of Dunkelflaute - low wind speeds and limited sunshine - has driven day-ahead electricity prices sharply higher in the last week. In Germany and France, prices have surged towards EUR 350/MWh, levels last seen during the 2022–23 energy crisis, while the UK and Nordic markets have also experienced sharp increases.

The spike highlights Europe's growing dependence on weather-driven renewable generation and the critical role of gas-fired power plants in balancing the grid when wind and solar output falter. With gas supplies already constrained and heating demand rising, the need for additional gas-fired generation is adding further pressure to an already tight market. The extreme price volatility also underscores the importance of dispatchable backup capacity, energy storage and cross-border interconnections as Europe continues its energy transition.
